gui.gonzotech.notes.title: Scholar's Notes
gui.gonzotech.notes.p1.title: Hello me
gui.gonzotech.notes.p1.body:
*"How do I put this... I — that is, you — am the old you. I wiped my, well, your memory. I don't plan on coming back: you're my living tombstone now. I hope you get a better life than I had... Good luck."*

Self — Gonzo:

Farewell, Gonzo...

To bring order to this mad world, the first thing I crafted was a chalkboard. It is My chief instrument of knowledge. Now I can see formulas before My eyes, balance equations, and make discoveries.

**By dragging blocks into an equation**, I immediately see the board's hints — it judges how precisely the elements are balanced.

If the balance accuracy **exceeds 90%**, it results in a full **Discovery**.

Here I can leave Myself notes and endlessly combine units, deriving new physical quantities. As I progress, the board will unlock harder problems and unknown constants.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p2.title: Observation
gui.gonzotech.notes.p2.body:
Watching the beasts, I noticed one odd thing: they often leave fruit in hollows, in grass or among leaves, and come back to it later.

Perhaps something happens to the fruit while it waits. I need to check.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p3.title: Fermentation
gui.gonzotech.notes.p4.title: Energy
gui.gonzotech.notes.p4.body:
Watching fire and water, I slowly came to one simple thought: in both cases energy can be obtained and passed on, if the process is organized right.

To keep the terms straight, I decided to call heat **GTH** (Gonzo Tech Heat) and pure energy — **GTU** (Gonzo Tech Units).

First I need a stable source of GTH. So I built a firebox and tried to get heat from plain combustion. We will see what can be done with it.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p5.title: Firebox and Boiler
gui.gonzotech.notes.p6.title: Stirling Generator
gui.gonzotech.notes.p6.body:
The firebox and the boiler work, but steam by itself is good for little. I decided to try a Stirling engine.

The principle turned out fairly simple: a temperature difference forces the pistons to move, and the motion can already be used to make **GTU**.

The problem was elsewhere — the boiler keeps losing water. It has to be topped up by hand, and it starts to get tiring quickly.

So the next step is to put the water back into the system.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p7.title: Condensation
gui.gonzotech.notes.p7.body:
Little by little it became clear where the water goes. Steam leaves the system, cools down, and never comes back on its own.

I built a condenser that cools the steam and returns the resulting water to the boiler. By rough estimates, each condenser returns 13% more water to the cycle.

Now the water no longer has to be hauled around by hand. There are still losses, but the system can almost run without interference.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p8.title: Closed Loop
gui.gonzotech.notes.p8.body:
Condensation cut the losses noticeably, but it did not solve the problem completely. Even in a closed system, water and energy slowly run out.

So I decided to stop trying to save every drop and instead spend a little **GTU** on bringing the water back.

For that I built an automatic pump. It takes water from an outside source and feeds it back into the system on its own.

Now it is a closed loop. It takes a little energy to run, but it no longer depends on constant manual refilling.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p9.title: Electric Smelting
gui.gonzotech.notes.p9.body:
When the energy was enough, I wanted to use it for more than just running the system itself.

I built an energy accumulator and an electric furnace. The accumulator slowly drains by itself, but I hope to fix that in the future. Compared to a plain furnace it works cleaner and lets me control the heat far more precisely…
gui.gonzotech.notes.p10.title: Logistics
gui.gonzotech.notes.p10.body:
When there were more machines, it became hard without proper logistics. To set up the network I made a spanner.

With it you can look inside the connected pipes and change their mode. 
A plain **right click** switches the flow direction: automatic mode, take, or give. 
**Shift + right click** is used to rotate the elements.

I split the system into several types: wires for **GTU**, pipes for water and steam, and separate lines for **GTH**. To join several directions I had to make distribution nodes.

It all fits fairly compactly, so the same network is easy to extend as new machines appear.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p11.title: Cobblestone Generator
gui.gonzotech.notes.p11.body:
I finally built a setup that makes cobblestone on its own and picks up some ore along the way.

It is the same water-and-**GTU** combination as before, only now the process is fully automated.

It runs quite stably, though it sometimes stops: the lava crystallizes into obsidian right in the bucket, and the pickaxe hits a tough inclusion and breaks. Apparently, perfect machines do not exist yet.

Still, this is the first of my setups that can be left unattended for at least a little while.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p12.title: Item Logistics
gui.gonzotech.notes.p12.body:
When there were more items in the system, one resource network was no longer enough. I made separate item logistics with pipes, nodes and filters.

The filter only lets through what is set into it. For everything else I added a scavenger — it takes the extra items and sends them down a different route.

Now the mined output can be split automatically right in the stream: what is needed goes to production, the rest — to processing or storage.

Nothing fundamentally hard, but there is a lot less manual sorting now.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p13.title: Item Logistics
gui.gonzotech.notes.p14.title: Universal Node
gui.gonzotech.notes.p14.body:
A separate node for every kind of stream quickly took up too much space.

So I reworked the scheme and built a universal node that can serve several kinds of streams at once.

The construction turned out noticeably more compact. Now I just need to properly solve the load on several directions at the same time.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p15.title: Steam Turbine
gui.gonzotech.notes.p15.body:
The Stirling works, but the pistons have an obvious limitation: the motion is jerky.

I decided to try a rotor scheme and aimed the steam straight at the blades. That is how the first version of the steam turbine appeared.

With several rotors it works well, but it cannot be grown forever. At some point further expansion stops helping, and then the output starts to fall.

So the size of a turbine has to be calculated in advance, not just built as big as possible…
gui.gonzotech.notes.p17.title: Machines and Redstone
gui.gonzotech.notes.p17.body:
I noticed a surprising ability of redstone: to read the state of a machine through a comparator. Now the machine itself can report when it is full and when something in the system needs to change.

Thanks to this, hatches can be opened automatically, single machines can be switched off, and accumulators can be kept from overflowing.

This surprising red dust, I am sure, still keeps many secrets...
gui.gonzotech.notes.p18.title: Ore Crusher
gui.gonzotech.notes.p18.body:
I wanted to get more useful material from ore blocks than plain smelting gives, so I built a crusher.

It breaks the ore block and separates the metal from the extra materials. And the result depends not only on the ore, but on the rock it was found in.

It turned out to be a rather convenient way to get rare components alongside the main metal.

It seems that when processing ore one should consider not only the ore, but the place it was mined from.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p19.title: Grinder II
gui.gonzotech.notes.p19.body:
After processing, a lot of metal dust is left. Throwing it away would be silly, so I made a separate grinder for a similar process.

It grinds clean ingots into dust without impurities — that will be the basis for mixing…
gui.gonzotech.notes.p20.title: Simple Metallurgy
gui.gonzotech.notes.p20.body:
Steel turned out to be quite easy to get from that very dust.

I mixed iron dust with coal and got steel dust. Then, the same way, I made several more alloys, simply changing the proportions of the starting materials.

That is how the first simple way to control a metal's properties through its composition appeared.

This is only the basic version. For more complex alloys a separate process will be needed — some metals cannot simply be mixed in a ratio and sent to the furnace…
gui.gonzotech.notes.p22.title: Press II
gui.gonzotech.notes.p22.body:
I reworked the press so that the same body can perform several operations.

For that I added two selector slots: one picks the form, the other does the pressing.

The plate form with a flat punch makes plates, the ingot form can squeeze dust into an ingot, the core form is needed for cores, and the wedge punch helps me slice ingots into wires.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p23.title: Alloy Foundry
gui.gonzotech.notes.p23.body:
With alloys I wanted to go further. I started to look at a metal not just as a material, but as a set of separate properties.

Depending on the composition, strength, hardness, conductivity, heat resistance and other characteristics change.

For that I built an alloy foundry, which mixes several metals into one. The final properties depend on which components were used and in what amounts.

Even the color comes from the composition, so from the alloy itself you can roughly tell what it is made of.

Some combinations take enchantments poorly. Apparently, high inertness has a perfectly practical downside...
gui.gonzotech.notes.p24.title: Centrifuge CF1UR
gui.gonzotech.notes.p24.body:
I made a centrifuge for a more detailed separation of ores.

Besides the main metal, it extracts the extra materials. That allows pulling far more useful components out of one ore than plain processing does.

The process uses hot water, which can be obtained from steam, or — for emergencies — I provided electric water heating with **GTU**.

Cesium is a different matter. Even the scheme of obtaining it stays dangerous, so that part of production is better kept separate from the rest of the system.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p25.title: Machines of the Second Generation
gui.gonzotech.notes.p25.body:
With the second generation of Machines I did not reinvent everything. The main constructions already work, so I simply boosted their throughput.

The new wires and pipes are rated for bigger streams, the accumulators hold more energy, the furnaces run faster, and the item logistics copes with larger volumes.

It is the same technology, but now suitable for big production lines.

The next limitation is no longer a single machine, but the organization of the system itself.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p29.title: Advanced Steam Generator
gui.gonzotech.notes.p29.body:
I made the advanced steam generator for the moments when the plain steam scheme is no longer enough.

At its heart are several cores and heat exchangers. With them, more steam can be gotten out of the same process, and the quality of the exchangers directly affects the result…
gui.gonzotech.notes.p30.title: Heart of the Steam Generator
gui.gonzotech.notes.p30.body:
Precious blocks are excellent heat exchangers: the sum of their heat resistance and conductivity directly affects the efficiency of the steam generator.

But it is easy to overdo the construction itself. If the exchangers are weak or few, the setup starts to spend more resources than the plain cycle.

So this is not a universal replacement for the old system...
gui.gonzotech.notes.p31.title: Nuclear Firebox
gui.gonzotech.notes.p31.body:
After all the experiments with heat, I finally built the nuclear firebox.

It allows getting a lot of **GTH** out of a small amount of nuclear fuel. The more heat accumulates inside, the harder it works.

The main problem is overheating. At too high a temperature the risk to the surrounding blocks grows, and if nothing is done, the firebox itself starts to fall apart.

So the cooling system had to be designed together with the firebox from the start. To take the extra heat away, I made a tungsten absorber.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p32.title: Redstone and Lava
gui.gonzotech.notes.p32.body:
During the redstone experiments I found another useful reaction.

If a full lava is aimed at a redstone block from the right side, both materials turn into **crimson obsidian**. From the top side the reaction does not happen.

Lava in a bucket behaves similarly on contact with water — the bucket's contents turn into obsidian.

I do not know yet how widely this can be applied, but the reaction is worth keeping in mind.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p33.title: Tungsten, the Great Absorber
gui.gonzotech.notes.p33.body:
After testing the nuclear firebox I needed a separate heat storage. For that I reworked the tungsten block into an absorber.

It connects to a heat pipe and takes the extra **GTH** out of the system. A superdense ice can be placed next to it — it noticeably speeds up the cooling.

The absorber itself has a limit. When overheated badly it becomes dangerous to the surrounding area, so it should not be left unattended.

For now this is the most convenient way to stabilize the nuclear system.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p34.title: Cesium, the Promise of an Explosion
gui.gonzotech.notes.p34.body:
Cesium turned out to be a terribly inconvenient material to work with.

I specifically checked its reaction with water — the result is predictably bad. In water, and when heated, it explodes, and the dust after processing behaves no better.

So a separate room for it had to be laid out before production even started.

The main rule with cesium is simple: no accidental contact with water.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p35.title: The Weakening Sun
gui.gonzotech.notes.p35.body:
Around the tenth day, the sun started behaving strangely.

The sky rose crimson — not a sunset, but properly crimson — and the sun came up red, dim, as if burned out. There was as much light that day as at dusk: monsters wandered the fields in broad daylight and burned only at high noon, when the crimson disc crossed the zenith.

There was no rain. There was snow — in every biome, even where it shouldn't be. The layers settled on fields and paths, and by the third morning everything around was white.

I checked the records: it repeats, and each time more often. The sun is cooling. I no longer ask why. Now I simply count the days until the next crimson dawn.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p36.title: Introduction to Deep Metallurgy
gui.gonzotech.notes.p36.body:
After the third discovery I began to understand metals much better, even though before I thought I had reached the limit of perfection. I literally see how my ingot got an exact numerical description: seven properties.

Strength — how well the material holds a load. More is better.

Brittleness — how easily it shatters. There is no 'more is better' here: somewhere around 30 is a fair margin, beyond that the material starts to crumble, but it digs faster and hits sharper.

Inertness — resistance to rust, corrosion, dissolving.

Conductivity — how well the material carries electricity. Or redstone signals

Heat resistance — at what temperature it still keeps its shape; above 75 the item does not burn in fire or lava.

Plasticity — how easily it can be pressed and bent, the antonym of brittleness.

Weight — how heavy the same volume is. Heavy items also dig stronger and hit harder, but the swing speed leaves a lot to be desired

Separately — the mining tier: the most I can dig up with it...
gui.gonzotech.notes.p37.title: Corten: Steel for Bad Weather
gui.gonzotech.notes.p37.body:
Ordinary iron does not live long outdoors — I needed an alloy that handles rust on its own.

19 portions of iron and 6 portions of additives — 3 copper, 1 chromium, 2 nickel. 25 portions per melt, 25 ingots.

Corten does not fight rust — it channels it. A dense layer of oxides grows on the surface, and the metal beneath is no longer eaten away. That is where the inertness 86 comes from: the rust reaches this layer and stops.

Strength 66, heat resistance 78, tier — iron. It sets no records, but rain and frost do not bother it.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p38.title: Stellite: The Strongest
gui.gonzotech.notes.p38.body:
I wanted to see how far strength can be pushed if you do not skimp on expensive additives.

6 parts cobalt, 3 chromium, 1 each of tungsten, coal and neodymium — 12 parts, 11 ingots per melt.

Strength 94 and heat resistance 96 — nothing I have made so far is higher. Inertness 92. Tier — netherite and above.

It did not come out cheap, but it turned out to be exactly what I wanted.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p39.title: Vitreloy: Metallic Glass
gui.gonzotech.notes.p39.body:
The idea was to make an alloy that solidifies faster than it has time to crystallize — then the structure stays glass-like instead of a lattice.

2 parts diamond, 2 ferromagnetic alloy, 3 zirconium and 2 nickel — 9 parts, 9 ingots per melt.

It turned out surprisingly well: inertness 96 — it cannot be higher, and conductivity 22 — nothing is lower. It bends poorly, barely carries current, but heat resistance 89 with strength 92. Tier — diamond, this alloy will clearly become indispensable to me for inert pipes with aggressive heat carriers.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p40.title: Semiconductor: The Foundation of Electronics
gui.gonzotech.notes.p40.body:
Pure silicon for electronics is hard to get — almost all of it goes to waste, and a grain is left.

One portion of neodymium, three portions of pure silicon, two portions of gold, one copper and three clay blocks, plus a radium nugget as a catalyst. And from this volume — only 4 ingots per melt.

Its strength is so-so: 22, brittleness 66 — holding a load is not what it is for. But conductivity 86, inertness 88, weight only 31: light and it does not rust. It does not like heat, though: heat resistance 55, electronics do not get along with heat at all.

Radium — a trace left after processing uranium and thorium ore, silicon — after diamond ore. Both through the centrifuge. Everything that 'thinks' on contacts begins with this alloy...
gui.gonzotech.notes.p26.title: Second-Tier Logistics
gui.gonzotech.notes.p26.body:
The second generation of logistics had to be made mainly because of the load.

I strengthened the wires and pipes, increased the throughput of the nodes, and added a way to properly split big streams between several directions.

The principle stayed the same, but now the network can be scaled without every extension turning into a rework of the whole scheme.

For large setups this is now an almost required update.
gui.gonzotech.notes.p28.title: Item Logistics 2
gui.gonzotech.notes.p28.body:
With item logistics it went about the same way.

First I gave the scavenger the ability to **delete unwanted** items. If it is **powered with redstone**, it switches to the **«deletion»** mode and burns everything the filter did not let through. I also increased the throughput of the pipes and the nodes and kept the same filtering and scavenging system, so a new control logic would not have to be invented.

Old schemes therefore transfer to the new version easily.

Now the amount of mining can be calmly increased, without constant manual sorting.
